claims.claim: Evagrius Ponticus was born in 345 in Ibora, Pontus, and died in 399 in Egypt.

Evagrius Ponticus was ordained as a reader by Basil of Caesarea and later served as a deacon and archdeacon under Gregory of Nazianzus in Constantinople, where he participated in the Second Ecumenical Council in 381.

Evagrius left Constantinople around 382, joined a monastic community in Jerusalem led by Rufinus and Melania the Elder, took monastic vows in 383, and then spent the rest of his life in the Egyptian desert at Nitria and Kellia.

The Expositio in Proverbia Salomonis (also known as Scholia on Proverbs) consists of approximately four hundred scholia, which are concise exegetical notes that do not provide continuous commentary but rather select passages from the book of Proverbs.

Evagrius's exegesis in the Scholia on Proverbs is almost exclusively spiritual, and can alternatively yield three meanings: ethical (practical), physical, and theological, corresponding to the trilogy of Solomon's books—Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and Song of Songs.
Evagrius's definition of a proverb is 'a sentence which designates intelligible realities by means of sensible realities.'
Evagrius frequently quotes John 15:15 in an abridged form in the Scholia on Proverbs, bringing together the antithetical terms servant and friend.
A manuscript of the Expositio in Proverbia Salomonis survives as Latin 465 in the Bibliothèque nationale de France.

Evagrius Ponticus was one of the most influential theologians in the late fourth-century church and developed the first major philosophical-theological exposition of monastic mysticism by developing the Neoplatonic biblical theology of Origen.

Evagrius's teachings were no longer considered orthodox in some strands of late ancient Christianity later in his life or after his death, although the Armenian and Syrian churches continued to cherish his writings.
